item.title: Optimizing Spring Boot App Performance
Spring Boot Database Connection Pooling
item.description:
When building a Spring Boot application that interacts with a PostgreSQL database, connection pooling is essential for improving performance. We've seen applications grind to a halt due to poor database connection management. To avoid this, we can use the HikariCP connection pooling library.
In your application.properties file, you can configure the connection pool like this: ```java spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb spring.datasource.username=myuser spring.datasource.password=mypassword spring.datasource.connectionTimeout=30000 ``` Then, in your configuration class, you can define a bean for the data source: ```java @Bean public DataSource dataSource() { return DataSourceBuilder.create() .driverClassName("org.postgresql.Driver") .url("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb") .username("myuser") .password("mypassword") .build(); } ``` This way, Spring Boot will manage the database connections for you and your application won't run out of connections.

item.title: Hosting Spring Boot on a ₹100 VPS without crashes
item.description:
Hosting Spring Boot on a cheap 512MB RAM VPS requires aggressive memory management. By default, the JVM acts greedy and grabs as much RAM as possible, which triggers the Linux OOM killer.
We can fix this by tuning three JVM flags in our startup script. We'll limit the Metaspace, switch to Serial GC and cap the heap. The Serial collector doesn't have the heavy memory overhead of G1GC, making it perfect for single-core instances.
Here is the optimized startup command:
```bash java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=64m -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xms128m -Xmx256m -jar app.jar ```
This keeps your Spring Boot app running stable on a tiny machine. You can easily run your API, PostgreSQL and a lightweight Redis cache on a single ₹100 VPS without crashes.

item.title: Scale Spring Boot on a ₹100 VPS with Virtual Threads
item.description:
If you host your Spring Boot app on a cheap ₹100 VPS, standard thread-per-request models will crash your server under load. Platform threads map 1:1 to OS threads and each thread eats up about 1MB of RAM. If you hit 200 concurrent requests, you waste 200MB of memory just on idle threads waiting for Postgres, Redis and external API calls.
Spring Boot 3.2 makes it incredibly easy to fix this. You don't need complex reactive programming. Just use virtual threads.
Add this to your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true ```
This single flag forces Tomcat to use JVM-managed virtual threads. When a request blocks on a database query, the underlying OS thread is released to do other work. Now, your tiny server can easily scale to thousands of concurrent requests without running out of memory.

item.title: Stop Using Default @Transactional for Read Queries
Optimizing Database Queries in Spring Boot
Stop letting HikariCP kill your cheap database
item.description:
When you host a Spring Boot app on a ₹100/month tiny server, the default HikariCP settings will crash your database.
By default, Hikari sets the maximum pool size to 10. If you run three microservices, that is 30 active connections. PostgreSQL allocates a separate process for each connection, eating up precious RAM on your small VM.
You don't need 10 connections for low-to-medium traffic. Shrink your pool size and decrease the timeout so threads don't wait forever.
Update your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=3 spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=1 spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000 spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=120000 ```
This setup handles hundreds of API requests per second by quickly reusing connections. It keeps your database RAM usage low and prevents PostgreSQL from running out of memory.

item.title: Stop Using Identity Generation for Batch Inserts in Spring Boot
Stop Letting HikariCP Kill Your Cheap VPS
item.description:
Most developers launch Spring Boot on a cheap ₹100/month VPS and wonder why it crashes. The silent killer is often the default HikariCP connection pool.
By default, Hikari sets the maximum pool size to 10. Each active database connection consumes precious memory on both your app and database. If you run PostgreSQL, Redis and Spring Boot on a single 1GB RAM instance, this default setup quickly triggers the Linux OOM killer.
If your app doesn't handle massive concurrent writes, scale down. Limit the pool size to 2 or 3.
Update your `application.properties`:
```properties spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=3 spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=1 spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=10000 spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=30000 ```
This small tweak keeps your database footprint tiny, prevents crashes and lets you host full-stack apps on dirt-cheap hardware while scaling your initial revenue.

item.title: Run Spring Boot on a $1 VPS with GraalVM
item.description:
If you're hosting Spring Boot on cheap VPS plans, memory is your biggest bottleneck. A standard JVM app easily consumes 300MB to 500MB of RAM just sitting idle. That kills your budget if you want to run multiple services on a single cheap server.
The fix is compiling your application to a native binary using GraalVM. This drops startup time to milliseconds and cuts RAM usage to under 50MB.
You don't need complex configurations. Just add the GraalVM native buildtools plugin to your `pom.xml`:
```xml <plugin> <groupId>org.graalvm.buildtools</groupId> <artifactId>native-maven-plugin</artifactId> </plugin> ```
Then build your native image:
```bash mvn -Pnative native:compile ```
The compiler analyzes your code statically and removes unused classes, reflection overhead and heavy JVM startup processes. Your app now runs lightning fast on a tiny VPS, saving you hosting costs while handling traffic.
